analysis.one_liner: Lets taxpayers donate $5 of their tax refund to fund IRS enforcement against high earners.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and attracted no cosponsors before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let taxpayers voluntarily check a box giving $5 of any tax refund to a new 'Taxpayer Fairness Fund.' The fund would pay for hiring IRS enforcement staff to track down unpaid taxes from people making over $500,000 a year and corporations with $5 million or more in assets. The bill was introduced in July 2020 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, ordinary taxpayers who pay what they owe would benefit, because the IRS would have more staff dedicated to auditing high earners and large corporations — groups that generally have more complex returns and more capacity to shelter income. Taxpayers who voluntarily contribute would see no personal gain; the benefit is a fairer system for everyone.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary taxpayers who pay what they owe

how_it_helps.text: The fund would finance the hiring, training, and employment of IRS personnel specifically to 'determine and collect owed taxes' from individuals with annual incomes of $500,000 or more and corporations with assets of $5 million or more.
Contributions are entirely voluntary: each taxpayer may designate $5 of a tax overpayment (refund) to the fund, with both spouses able to designate on a joint return.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers who choose to give up $5 of their refund, and potentially high-income individuals and large corporations who would face more IRS collection activity — the enforcement the bill is designed to fund would be aimed squarely at them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Voluntary donors and wealthy tax evaders

drawbacks.text: A voluntary $5 checkoff is an unstable and very small funding base for tax enforcement. By general analogy to the well-known presidential campaign checkoff, the share of taxpayers who voluntarily check such boxes is small, and enforcement staffing requires sustained, predictable appropriations that year-to-year voluntary donations cannot guarantee.

The bill excludes from contributing any recipient of the Earned Income Tax Credit, Child Tax Credit, or American Opportunity Tax Credit — the very low- and middle-income taxpayers the fund's stated purpose is meant to serve, and the largest group of refund recipients.
The amount dedicated is tiny ($5 per return, per spouse) relative to the scale of IRS enforcement needs, so the bill as written could not produce a meaningful expansion of audits on its own.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea points in the right direction — using IRS enforcement to collect taxes already owed by high earners and large corporations — but the design is weak: a voluntary $5 checkoff cannot fund serious enforcement, and predictable appropriations would do the job better. The bill's cost to the public is negligible since contributions are voluntary, but its practical benefit would also have been small. In any case, it never advanced far enough for the design question to matter.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went straight from introduction to the House Ways and Means Committee's Subcommittee on Select Revenue Measures on the same day, sat there with no cosponsors, and died when Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Gwen Moore (D-WI) introduced the Taxpayer Fairness Fund Act of 2020 on July 16, 2020.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means and then to its Subcommittee on Select Revenue Measures.
No further action was taken; the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 without the bill receiving a hearing, a mark-up, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income individuals and large corporations whose complex tax situations would have faced additional IRS scrutiny are better off, since no new enforcement funding was created. The IRS also gains nothing it lost — its funding stays where it was — but taxpayers hoping for more enforcement against the wealthy gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners and large corporations facing audits

sides.party_line_note: No one ever voted on the bill and it drew no cosponsors, so no partisan lineup on the merits ever emerged — the bill simply never moved out of committee.

industries.industry: High-income individuals and large corporations facing IRS collection
industries.note: The bill would fund IRS personnel specifically to determine and collect owed taxes from individuals earning $500,000+ and corporations with $5 million+ in assets. More enforcement means more audits and collections against these groups, which is exactly the money ordinary taxpayers otherwise effectively shoulder through the tax gap.
The bill creates a dedicated fund for hiring and training IRS enforcement staff. Tax administration and collection is a listed subject of the bill.
